new_statements.quote: There are two tonemes: high tone and low tone, which though contrastive carry a low semantic load. Only a few grammatical stems contrast with reference to pitch alone, and then only in certain frames [...] (p. 211) The nucleus of the phonological phrase is identified by the length of the vowel of the syllable or of the consonant following the vowel, or of both. The nucleus of a phrase is always the first syllable of a grammatical stem. The length of this syllable varies; longer length is accompanied by a tendency for the pitch to glide. [...] The phonological clause [...] is characterized by an onset of indrawn breath, a peak of accent on the nucleus of one of the first two phonological phrases, and heavy exhaling or breathiness at closure. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kensinger treats Cashinahua as a two-tone language (high vs. low, low functional load) and does not state a word-stress rule; the closest equivalent is that the prominent (length-marked) nucleus of each phonological phrase is always the first syllable of a grammatical stem, i.e. stem-initial prominence, with a clause-level accent peak on one of the first two phrase nuclei. Older and later sources disagree: Capistrano de Abreu 1914 (Brazilian Caxinauá of the Ibuaçu, p. 13) gives fixed final stress ('O accento tónico recai sempre na ultima vogal, excepto si ha ditongo'), and Oisel et al. 2024 (fn. 17, Peru) treat stress as lexically variable (words ending in a stressed vowel vs. yawa with initial stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Kensinger: each successive phrase nucleus in a clause is progressively shorter than the one bearing clause accent (p. 211).
new_statements.exceptions: Kensinger: tone perturbations not analysed; borders of phrases 'often fuzzy'. Abreu 1914: diphthongs take the accent on their first element; notes variation ka-xi-nau-á ~ ka-xi-náu-a and penultimate accent in Madeira/Ucayali Pano languages. Oisel et al. 2024: stress position differs lexically (final vs. initial) and conditions genitive allomorphy.
new_statements.domain_note: Kensinger's units are phonological phrase and clause, not the word; the stem-initial prominence statement is about phrase nuclei (grammatical stem = word-level unit). Abreu's statement is word-level (citation forms elicited from two speakers). Varieties: Kensinger = Curanja River, Peru (with an Embira, Brazil speaker); Abreu = Ibuaçu/Muru (Tarauacá), Brazil; both are cash1254 per Fleck 2013's index.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources are cash1254 [cbs]. Kensinger 1963 describes the Peruvian Curanja River Cashinahua (with an Embira/Brazil speaker showing no differences); Capistrano de Abreu 1914 describes the Brazilian Caxinauá of the Rio Ibuaçu/Muru (Tarauacá), which Fleck 2013's index equates with Cashinahua [cbs] (distinct from the extinct 'Kashinawa of the Tarauacá River', Glottolog NOCODE); Kaxinawá 2014 and Oisel et al. 2024 describe the Brazilian (Acre) and Peruvian varieties respectively.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Kensinger 1963 statement (phrase nucleus = first syllable of a grammatical stem, marked by length) and adds only that Peruvian Cashinahua has an unstressed-syllable environment for d/n allophony in which initial syllables are exempted; no placement claim of its own. new_statements.rule_in_words: No stress placement rule. The alphabet note presupposes a stressed/unstressed distinction (d > n in unstressed non-initial syllables) but gives no rule for where stress falls. Nothing on tone or vowel length; the Tomo II grammatical appendix excerpt (Rosetta) has no stress or accent term; the sil.org open_url (show_work.asp?id=563) is HTTP 404, so the archive.org copy was used.
new_statements.identity_note: Kaxinawá 2011 and 2014 describe Brazilian Hãtxa kuĩ / Huni kuĩ (Acre; 2011 data from aldeia Mibãyã, T.I. Carapanã) and both note that Camargo's data are mainly Peruvian Hãtxa kuĩ (2011 p. 71; 2014 p. 150-151). Montag 1981 and the unreached Montag 1979 / Cromack 1968 describe Peruvian Cashinahua (SIL Peru, Curanja/Purús). Kensinger 1963 (the catalog's existing statement) is also Peruvian. sources.note: Whole paper is phonology (Pike-style hierarchy). p.211 sec.5: two contrastive tonemes (high, low) with low semantic load; p.214 sec.7: the phonological-phrase nucleus is marked by vowel/consonant length and 'is always the first syllable of a grammatical stem'; sec.8: clause has 'a peak of accent on the nucleus of one of the first two phonological phrases'. No word-stress rule stated as such. Data: Curanja River, Peru; an Embira (Brazil) speaker showed no differences.
